subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
That may be. I do not want to take my line of conduct in any respect from Germany. I want democracy, I want democratic government apd democratic principles, but in time of war, when we have a responsible Administration charged with the conduct of the war, we are perfectly justified in putting a measure through in short order and carrying it out as a matter of administration. To-day, a government that believes in conscription is asked to go to the people and get their approval in connection with this measure. What we have .to do is to allow the Government to carry on the war and put the responsibility upon them when the time comes.
There is a corollary which follows what I have just said. What is it? We had a peace government in this country when war began. We have carried on the war for three years and we are now beginning to have a war government. The people think that the time has arrived when we should have a national government, a union government, a coalition government, if you care to call it such, to carry on the war. The trouble in Canada to-day is that we have not got a united government. We only have a government so far on party lines. There has been a proposal in the country, and it has been referred to in the House, to get a union government. We have to get that union government to carry on the war and to enforce this Act. I started out to talk about how we were to enforce the Act and I discussed the question of money and of the officer who was responsible for its enforcement. But we must have a union government to enforce vthip Act. The people demand it and my hon, friends on the other side of the House who voted for conscription showed that they had heard the voice of the people demanding the enforcement of this conscription Act. They want to see it put through in short order. There are three things that the people of this country want -first, conscription, second, a union government, and, third, and above all things, to avoid an election in which political passions are called into play in this time of war. In some way or other, we want to see national unity but it is a hard thing

to get. I do not despair of that unity and the way to get it is to begin with a national government, a government representing all the people who are in favour of com scription. We cannot get them all but in war tjme, if we are bound to win the war, if we want to create national unity, or at least unity among all those who believe in conscription, we must have a national government on that line. I hope national government will come and that it will be made up of those who are in favour of a national policy to win the war and of devoting all the energies of the people to that end. I do not think Canada is going to be disrupted on this question by reason of this proposal for conscription. What you want is vigour and strength in doing what ought to be done and the responsibility for that is on the Administration. The Administration then ought to go forward with the law that does require what should be done, a law that has to be enforced and, above all a law that will be enforced and upheld by a national government.
We must'come to that in this country; we must come to it within the next six weeks or I do not know what is going to happen. There will be dissension in this country, because there are to-day signs of a lack of unity. But there are also growing signs of national co-operation among the different parties in this country. The speeches that have been made in this House by hon. gentlemen on the other side in favour of conscription have only reflected the opinion of the people of this country, and this House must be as big as the people. But we are not. The people of Canada are largely in favour of this law; they are in favour of its enforcement; they are in fav.oux of unity and co-operation, and not of political dissension. We are making headway in that line to-day and we have been for a good many days past. The people are with us. They desire to have this Parliament reflect their views and establish a national government which will help to build up and strengthen national unity. They also want, above all things, to have all the resources of the country devoted to the winning of the war, this to be worked out on lines of administration. This is not a time to discuss questions of principle that should have been settled and were settled in this country years ago, when the present Militia Act was passed. We have undertaken in this time of war to re-discuss a principle that was settled long ago, a principle which we have no business to be discussing" to-day. The Administration here should be as strong as the Administration in England has been since the establishment of a national government. That Government oame down' and said: Here is a conscription measure which we propose to put into force. We want Parliament to pass it within a few days. That was done in England and it was done in the United States, and these are both democratic governments, just as much ,as ours is. We can learn from them a good many things about how to conduct a democratic government, even in war times. But the characteristic of all governments in war times ought to be administration and not discussion. The Government has assumed the responsibility and can easily discharge it if they will rise to the point-and the Prime Minister has risen to the point-of proposing a national government. If that is done, there will be no trouble in enforcing this law. I d>o not want to see this discussion prolonged. I want to see the law placed on the statute book and to see it enforced, and I want to see a union Government to enforce it. If that is done we will get the 100,000, or any number of men we have to get. We will get them in some way, and a union Government will have no trouble in getting them. With a union Government there will be no delay in administering the law; it will go right ahead with it. If we can do that on this occasion there will be very little disunion in the country, there will be, on the Contrary, a splendid display of national union, all our people joining together in a mighty effort to win the war. We are fighting for principles which we hold dear, the principles of liberty. Every nation now in the war is working on the principle of conscription.

That it is expedient in the national interest that the man should, instead of being employed in military service, be engaged in other work in which he is habitually engaged.

The consequence is that the Government will get many more men from that class than they expect, and it- is a pity and a shame that those boys should be taken away and the other men from 23 to 28 and from 28 to 34 should not be drawn upon at the same time.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
If the hon. member
thinks the matter out, he will come to the conclusion that even if his prediction is correct

and I think that is very unlikely

speechtext: My hon. friend takes the wrong meaning out of what I said. I do not mean to say it is a shame that some shpuld be taken and some left. subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
If the hon. gentleman
will think longer I may be wrong and he may be right. However, just let me put this to him. If his prediction is right under his plan there will be, say, two boys, .as he calls them, in the same position, both 23 years of age. Smith will be taken for the "front, and Jones will he left at home.

speechtext: You dp that anyway.

speechtext:
What we do is this:
we take Smith and Jones, but we leave at home for the time being Brown and White, who are between 24 and 28. According to my hon. friend's plan he would take Smith and White, pne in the first class and one in the second class. 1 Now I am not sure that 'Smith would feel any better at the front because Brown was left at home than he would feel if Jones was left at home.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: That applies all around, no matter how you select them.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: The only difference is that Jones is the same age as Smith, and cannot see any reason why Smith should be left at home. White is a few years older, and there may be something in leaving him at home for the time being.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
I quite agree with my hon. friend from North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt). In the stress of war as war is waged at the present time, I am thoroughly convinced that the men between 24 and 28 years of age, as defined by class No. 2, are physically better able to withstand the trials. They are more mature, and are able to stand the hardships better than the young men of 20. They are also betteT able to withstand the temptations of a soldier's life, and we all know this is a very serious phase at any time. While I can quite agree with what has been advanced by the Solicitor General on previous days, that the men between 24 and 28 would probably make a slightly bigger hole in the affairs of the country if they were taken away, because of the fact that a man between 24 and 28 is more likely to be established in life, still I think it is absolutely certain, as my hon. friend from North Oxford says, if you want to get 50,000 men in the first draft you may get every one of them in class No. 1, from 20 to 24 years of age, and you may have a great many in the same class left. I think it would be an absolute mistake to take 50,000 men from the men between 20 and 24 years of age. I should think it

would be much better to unite these three classes, Nos. 1, 2, and 3, into one class, and call them out together, and select your 50,000 men or 70,000 men from them. I believe 70,000 was the number mentioned by my right hon. friend the Prime Minister. In that way you would get the men from 20 to 35 years of age, and would not get them all between 20 and 24. There is a great deal in what my hon. friend from North Oxford has said, and I think it is well worth while allowing the matter to stand over so that the Solicitor General may look into it further with a view to seeing if he cannot unite those three classes.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: The hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) has, it must be agreed, hit upon the real test as to whether selection should be made from the younger men first or those a little further on in life, namely, the test of fitness for the endurance of the war. His judgment of the fitness of the men, however, differs from that of the responsible leaders at the front. Sir Douglas Haig has very clearly stated that the men who endure the hardships of this war best are the men between 18 and 25. I am no judge of that myself, but if I were asked I should say I hardly think this possible. However, that is his statement. Then, there is another very important matter. The air service, which requires a physically perfect man, not only from the standpoint of health but from the very vital standpoint of nerve strength, restricts its men to the ages 18 to 25. These two considerations seem to me to put it beyond the discussion of this House as to what class of men really endure the hardships of this war best. That being the case, it would appear to me that other considerations are secondary, although they are important. I want to add this, under this Bill if it is felt after a very thorough canvassing of the situation that the whole number can be secured in the first class, or for any other reason if it is felt that there will be little difficulty in proceeding with the selection under the tribunalls which have been inaugurated, we might very well call out class 1 on Monday, class 2 on Tuesday, and class 3 on Wednesday. For that matter, I think we might call one at nine o'clock, one at ten, and the third at eleven, on the same day.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
Might I call attention to the United States Act placed on the Table to-day, which reads:
Such draft as herein provided shall be based upon liability to military service of all 
male citizens, or male persons, not alien enemies, who have declared their intention to become citizens, between the ages of 21 and 30 years, both inclusive.
. Mr. MEIGHEN: I know that is the United States Act.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
I am rather inclined to fall in with the view ci the member for North Oxford in regard to the classes as they are placed here.
I think, notwithstanding the statement alleged to have been made by General Haig, and having regard to the fact that our soldiers are citizen soldiers and the common knowledge that one has that a boy of twenty is after all hardly a man but only a bpy, that his physical being has not been perfected and that his bones are not probably any too well set, there is something a little repellent and repulsive about the idea of putting an immature youth into a war of the nature of the present one. It is true that these young men have gone and it is splendid that they have gone willingly. Lots of them went at 16 years of age without any conscription. But it struck me while the discussion was going on that if class two were put where class one is, having regard to the argument that the force may be found in one or other of these classes, if the more seasoned, yet young, men were put first in class one and the younger boys put in class two, it would be following along a line that would be congenial to my thought and I believe would be very well received in the country. Wie all hear of Germany being forced to put her young men in the field. The Government might ameliorate the situation by making a different classification that would not prejudice the working out of the Bill. The Solicitor General says that all of these three classes will be required. If that is so the reversion of the numbers, putting number two where number one is, probably putting number three where number two is and putting number one where number three is, making number one the last of the classes, I believe would be a change that would not injure the working out of the Bill but would give to the first draft a full man's strength of those first selected, men steadier in their characters, more set ip their frame and constitution, and more calculated to endure the rigours of war.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
Would the Solicitor
General tell me why there has been a departure from the English Act? He has been good enough to lay on the table of the House the two British Acts and in looking over these I can only find one class-from 18 to 41 years of age. Am I right in that?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: The Solicitor General has spent hours quoting what has 'been done in England for our instruction and example. In fact, our Bill in many respects follows the English Act, and yet in England their experience shows them that it is wise only to have one class running from 18 to 41 years of age, making no distinction between married men and unmarried men. Yet, in this Bill the measure is complicated by creating ten different classes, which seem to be founded upon an arbitrary age limit for which there is apparently no good reason whatever. I would like to know why it is that the British Act has been so greatly departed from in that particular?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
I am not obliged, even in this instance, to depart from my veneration for British precedent. In Great Britain the Derby system was in effect for some time and a pledge was given by the then Pfime Minister to the married men who had enlisted that before they were sent overseas -I may not be precisely stating it-the unmarried man would be required. The first Military Service Act of Great Britain was for the purpose of carrying out that purpose in the main. The whole number between 18 and 41 were taken, but the Act applied there only to unmarried men, not to married men at all. Later on it was made applicable to married men. In the circumstances public opinion in Great Britain had reached such a position and the position of the Government as to the requirements in France had reached such a condition that they knew that they would need every one and perhaps more than every one they could possibly get. Consequently their Act covered them all together, but their Act provided what our Act does not provide, and I would like hon. gentlemen to note this, that they might be called out as would be set out in regulations. There they had the power by regulations to make the divisions. They divided according to age in Great Britain. Those first were all taken and after that they took them in order of age 'by regulation, commenting with-
' Air. PUGSLEY: What age?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Eighteen.

speechtext: What was the first class?

The voluntarily attested men will, as hitherto, be divided into groups according to their age and marital condition. The men to whom the Act applies will be divided into classes corresponding to the groups of single men who have voluntarily attested.
These voluntary attestations were according to age and those called put under the Military Service Act were called out in classes corresponding to the ages of the c.onscripts called out under the voluntary system.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wish to endorse the arguments which have been offered in favour of combining the first three classes under this Bill. I agree with what the hon. member for North Perth (Mr. Alorphy) has said about the greater suitability of those covered by the second class for the service which we require from these young men in a war of the kind in which we are engaged. Prom the military standpoint, I know that we would have much better service out of these three classes by combining them than by taking them singly in any order. It is -quite true that Sir Douglas Haig is>
reported to have said that the very best service has been secured from the youngest men in the army, but I am quite satisfied that neither Sir Douglas Haig nor any other general officer, would be satisfied to have his battalion composed exclusively of these young men. We need the young men to give steam to the operations -and we need the older men to give ballast. We have heard a great deal about the number of Canadians sent across to the Old Country and returned to Canada as rejects, as physically unfit. My experience is that that has been caused largely by the system they have there, particularly in the winter season, of discarding the very young and the very oldest classes of the Canadian Expeditionary Force.
Then, having got all these old men together, they send a large number of them back to Canada as unfit, -and having got the hoy-s together, they decide that they are not useful either and -send them back or

keep them for a -very long period. If they were sent as battalions with the old and the young and the middle aged together, they would have for the military service
1.000	fit men, whereas, by the process of elimination that now goes on during the winter months, they have only 800 fit men and 200 rejects.
It seems to me that we would get much better service if we would combine the three classes first named in this Bill, and that the authors of the 'Militia Act who provided for the calling out first of all men from eighteen to thirty, based their decision very wisely.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: From my hon. friend's experience, how long will it take these conscript troops before they are ready for the field?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
From my own experience in Canada, I may say that I had a battalion fully trained and ready for any experience that might be before it in six months from the date of authorization. We were kept in Canada after that for four months because of the falling off in recruiting. f In June of last year the 131st Battalion was over the 1,000 mark, that being the. strength supposed to. be attained before >a battalion was permitted to go overseas. From June until October the conditions for recruiting were so difficult, even in British Columbia, that we go.t new men only sufficient to meet the wastage in Canada, and when we got the order to go overseas in October we were only two over the
1.000	mark. Our training then was no. better than it was in June, when we first reached the 1,000. We were noit any better, probably we were a little stale if anything from discontent on the part of ithe men. When we got to England the battalion was found ready for any service, and the first draft of 500 men was sent to France within two weeks of our arrival in England.
'Mr. GRAHAM: I think that if anything were needed to convince the House of the wisdom of the combination of these two clauses, the member for New Westminster (Mr. Taylor) has provided that argument. I feel very strongly on this point, as I outlined the cither day. I am not sure that I would not make the minimum age twenty-one. This is not voluntary service; this is compulsory 'service, and we cannot base what we are going to do under this Act on anything that has occurred under 'voluntary service. You are compelling men to go, which is a far different thing from having them enlist. They can enlist at eighteen if they like. But there is a lot in what

niy hon. friend has said and also in the remarks of the hon. member for North Perth (Mr. Morphy) and the hon. member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt). No person need tell a man who has raised boys that the boy at twenty is ias well 'seasoned as a man at twenty-five. I do not care	what kind of theory you give,
we know better. Any man wber is engaged in athletics knows that a man do.es not play out at twenty-two or twenty-three, but is at his best at twenty-five o.r twenty-six. Any man who engages men to go to the bush or elsewhere to endure hardships does not want the boys. As the hon. member for New Westminster says, the young man is aggressive, aggressive, perhaps, to recklessness, and I agree that no commander would want a battalion of that kind unless he had the steadiness of the older men with theop. Leaving out the domestic side of it-'because taking a boy of twenty years of age from home by compulsion is a serious thing-to my mind no argument has been presented to show that the man of twenty is preferable to the older man. I have no hesitation in saying that no such argument can be presented. He is not mature.
There is another side of it. It has been stated as the intention of this Bill to take men who are not needed in this country, that is men who are lees needed than others and who are not producing, but are rather consuming what others produce. If you go through the large cities and comb them to find out the men who are doing this thing, it will be found that they are not men between twenty and twenty-four, that -more of them are between twenty-four and thirty. The young man of twenty to twenty-four is probably a student and perhaps resides at home, just getting ready for life. If men are going to be non-producers, you will find them between twenty-four and twenty-eight. I agree with the hon. member for North Perth (Mr. Morphy); I would reverse number two and number one at least. That would be my first suggestion. But, better than that, I would combine the three classes that have been named-first, -second and third. In that vray I think the desired number of men would be easily obtained, probably in this one class, and I have yet to be convinced that a better and more seasoned class of men would not be got with these three classes combined than you vyill get under the first class alone.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
I would also suggest
to the Solicitor General to consider whether

he should not change the minimum age in class one to twenty-one years instead of twenty, making the minimum age one year more than at present. If we were short of men I would not make that suggestion; if there Was going to be any difficulty in getting. 100,000 men in Canada under this Bill, I would not think of making that suggestion. But there is not going to be any difficulty in getting the men, and I think every one will agree that a young man of twenty-one is better able to meet the exigencies of a soldier's life than the man who is a year younger. I think it would be an advantage to leave the boy at home until he is twenty-one years of age.
Mr. -GLASS:	There are two reasons for
giving consideration to the proposal to change the minimum age limit to twenty-one years of age: In the first place, we would be following the precedent set by the United States; in the second place, we wp-uld be responding to public opinion in this country. I have received requests from a number of organizations, women's organizations and others, urging that the -minimum age be placed at twenty-one, and I understand that the 'Government have received similar requests, some from my own district. The arguments -that have been presented by the hon. member for North Perth and the hon. member for New Westminster strongly impress on my mind the desirability of combining these three classes. Then it will be necessary to combine classes four, five and six, because they stand in exactly the same relation, only they happen to be married instead of single men. But, so far as the physical powers of the men are concerned, these classes are on all fours with classes one, two and three. I think the suggestion is a good one, and there should be no difficulty in getting the full complement from these three classes.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
I do not pretend to set myself up as an authority before the committee, as to when a man is most physically capable of standing the hardships of this war, first, because I am not an authority on physical fitness, and, secondly, because I do not know anything about the hardships of the war, and I would not think of placing my opinion against that of hon. gentlemen, especially those hon. gentlemen who have had as much to do with the militia as the hon. member from North Perth and the hon. gentleman from New Westminster. I want to call the attention of the committee to the fact that, in Great Britain, they divide them according to age, but that was not because
they expected to take all from the first age, namely, those born in 1899. That would be taking men who were only at that time 17 years of age. It was done merely for the convenience of enlistment. They knew, from the beginning, that they would require all of those ages that they could get. We are of the same opinion, and it is our intention to take, as I expressed it yesterday, those best available, wherever they are, . and of whatever age they are. But we want to start at this age for this reason: under the Bill, if those first three classes are grouped, which is suggested by several, it will mean that all of them will he called at once, and they will all come before the local tribunal at the same time.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
My hon. friend said he could call one class at nine o'clock, another at ten and another at eleven o'clock the same day. Would that not be the same condition? .
Mr. MElGHEN: Yes, that could be done, but it is in the public interest that we should he enabled to make the classes as they made them in England. They may be made in the United States in that way for similar reasons, under regulations.	All
men are made liable there, and all men are made liable here. We go further than the British and United States legislation, and we make classes ourselves, which, if all three were called together, would mean that all would come before	the
local tribunal on the day named in. that call. That would mean the withdrawal from their ordinary avocation of all these men at once, and the reporting to these tribunals on the day fixed for reporting in the proclamation. We might get, by that means, far more than, the alloted number. We want to avoid that if we can, but we also wish to avoid congestion of the tribunals, and the withdrawal from other avocations of life of everybody at once. We expect to require three classes. We may require four. Our expectations are not founded on anything that could be called sufficient data, but the purpose is to call some on. one day, some on another, and some on a third day, and then to select from all these, but we do not wish to he compelled to call all at once, because it will be likely to result in the congestion of the tribunals, and it will unnecessarily call away at one time all these men from the ordinary avocations of life, and create a very unnecessary disturbance.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: But they are only called out to report.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: And to apply for exemption.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: The great majority will not apply for exemption.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: The hon. Solicitor General informed the House, in answer to a question, that nobody appeared before the tribunal, except the men who wanted exemption.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: My statement was correct.	.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: How does it come that every one of these men will have to appear before the tribunal?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: I said all who wanted exemption would have to apply to the tribunal, and we feel it will not be convenient that they should be all called at once, because if they were, there might, and likely would, result a congestion of the work of the tribunal, and there would be an unnecessary withdrawal, at the same time, from the ordinary avocations of life of these men, some for the purpose of entering their applications for exemption, and others for the purpose of reporting, and all, ultimately, who are enlisted, for the purpose of recording. They could not all be taken at once very well. If the Bill read, "all who would he called upon" and that they might >be called upon, as set out in the regulations, then we could follow what they do in Great Britain, and likely what they will do in the United States. But we go further, .and do not ask the House'to trust to regulations. We set out the divisions in the Bill, not that we feel we will get the men from one division at all, because we want to comb the available men at all events from the first three divisions, and if we find that we do not get enough from those divisions we will have to comb from the married men, tout if we group the three classes the hon. gentlman from South Oxford will see it will mean the bringing in of all these men to report at once, the withdrawal of them from their avocations, and the bringing in of all who seek exemption, to make their applications to conduct the prosecution of their appeals, and so on. It will cause an unnecessary disturbance of. industry and withdrawal from ordinary pursuits.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Can my hon. friend tell me the number that would be lost by raising the age from 20 to 21?

speechtext:
I discussed that before.
I do not know that I can add anything to 
what I said the other day. I am not anxious to make the age 21, even for the sake of following American precedent.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Following our advice.

speechtext: The American precedent has been urged. subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Those that went at 18 are now 21, if they went at the beginning of the war.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: No.

speechtext: My hon. friend says he does not agree with me. I am assuming that is the case. If only the men who are asking for exemption are really to be interfered with, it makes little difference whether they are interfered with on Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday or Thursday.

speechtext: And the putting of these three classes together might make some little difference in the manner suggested by the Solicitor General, but so little as to be unobservable, or practically no difference at all in comparison with the magnitude of the work in hand.

speechtext: It just means three times the delay at the tribunal offices, and three times the crowding at the recording offices.

speechtext:
I do not think that is a serious objection. If necessary, there can be a greater number of tribunals. I think tftat would be one solution. I do not look

at it as my hon. friend does. I do not anticipate a mighty throng coming before these tribunals to seek exemption. I believe that the majority of young men will not seek exemption unless there be some real, tangible reason why they should do so; the number who ask for exemption will be comparatively small. But if what the Solicitor General apprehends does occur, and there is a little congestion, that circumstance sinks into insignificance when compared with the advantage of putting these three classes in on?.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: We get the same results in the end.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
If my hon. friend gets
the same results he will get the same congestion, but he will spread it over a few days longer.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Oh, n.o.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
The Solicitor General
thinks that he is not going to get the required number of men from the first , and second classes; that he will have to call out all three classes. If that be the case, I see no reason why they should not be all called out at once. 'I do, however, see a reason why all the eligible young men in Canada between the ages of 20 and 24 should not be taken while the others are left. If, as the Solicitor General argues, it' will be necessary to call out classes one, two and three in order to obtain the required number of men, then he has presented no argument to the committee why the three classes should not be combined in the first instance and called out in the same draft-unless it be that of congestion or of taking men from our industries, But it will not take a single man from the industries for a day or for a minute-only the men who are asking for exemption.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
What about the reporting of the men? They would all report on the same day if they were all called out at once; there would be just three times as much reporting, and it would take days to look after that part of it. . When I rise in the morning I am reasonably sure that I will require three meals on that day, but I do not on -that account argue that I ought to take the whole three at breakfast time because, although some congestion n)ight occur, I would get the same result. If we do nothing else, we avoid inconvenience by following the plan suggested in the Bill. Hon. gentlemen do not seem to realize that we can under the Bill obtain
the same result, because we can 10 p.m. see that all three are called out and that different dates, perhaps not far apart, are fixed for the hearing by the tribunals and the reporting of each of the three classes. In that war not one single object is lost that would be gained by having all report at once and the tribunals sit on all at once.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
If my hon. friend is
wrong in saying that the whole three classes will have to be called in order to secure the required number of men, under the Act as it stands he will denude Canada of the younger men and not touch the others at all. If he gets the required number of men between the ages of 20 and 24, he will not call out the others. I do not want to quote Germany as an example, but Germany, perhaps the greatest fighting machine in the world, calls out her boys last.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
Excuse me. Germany's
first army consisted of men under 24 years of age. The hon. gentleman should know that if he knows anything at all about it.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
I know that my hon.
friend knows everything-in his own mind -and that is just as good to him as really knowing. He will allow me to disagree with him ; there are many things even about the Canadian militia that he has yet to learn. If he will read the newspapers he will see that during the last few months Germany has resorted to calling out her boys.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Under, the military age.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
That depends on what
the military age is. But, whatever the military age is, I was referring to boys. No matter what my hon. friend says about the age of 24, I was talking about boys of 20. Germany calls out all her 'boys last; unless the cables are untrue she has called them out during the last few months.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
I have a book here, the
Here is what this year-book says, page the facts. I do not ask the hon. gentleman or the committee to accept my word for it. Here is what this Year-Book says, page 945, with reference to the German Empire and its state of defence:
Military service in Germany is compulsory and universal, with the usual exemptions. Liability commences at the age of 17 and ends at 45, hut actual service begins at 20. The term of service in the First Line, or active army, is seven years, two in the ranks and five in the reserve.

So that the first army in the trenches would consist of men from 20 to 22 years of age.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: That does not follow.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: We will agree, then, that the age goes up to 27. Rut the reason why boys are called out no.w is because every year a certain number of them reach the age of 17, 18 or 20, as the case may be. Every year the Auistro-German army gets over 800,000 additional men because that number of men become of age to enter the army. Tihe young men may be called out at 19, at 18, or at 17-because they become liable to service.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
At wharf, age are the
men of the German Empire put in reserve?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: At the age of 23 they go into reserve and serve there for five years. The army comprised of men from 20 to 23 was the First Line army that fought the British at Mons. The reserves were called out and embodied while the first army was marching across the frontier. Then the first army was embodied for a month, or, say, two or three weeks. Then the second army or reserve was embodied, now1 ready for the field, bringing all the men between 23 and 27 into the army.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
My hon. friend has said
lot of things that are not stated in that book.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
I am merely stating what I know to be the facts. I happened to meet some of the Germans over there, and I realized that the first German army was composed entirely of young men. Indeed, the German writers claim that men from 20 to 23 are the best soldiers.
When the First Contingent went over, a great number of men went who were under age. I do not say this to disparage the men under 20 who went to the front; no braver men ever fought for our King and country than the boys of 18. One who was a page on the floor of this House and who enlisted when the war broke out-he was then 16 years of age-is now a veteran who has seen service during two years and a half. The young men under 20 fought just as well as the men of 35 or 25. Moreover, they recovered their strength and spirits after a long day's march much more quickly than men 30 years of age. There is no reason why a man could not be enlisted to serve at the -age of 18 and be just as good a soldier as the man of 25. I should not want the committee to say that these men do not
rMr. Currie.]
fight well; many of them died bravely, standing their ground just as well as the older men. I have in mind oneyoung man who was 16 when the war broke out. He lied about his age, went to the front, was wounded in battle, came home, re-enlisted after recovering, assisted in recruiting a battalion, went back to the front with his battalion, and is being held in England for another six months until he reaches the age of 19. Further, if you are going to call out no men younger than 21, what about the number of volunteers, who are in the Old Country waiting until they reach the age of 19? There is some force in what the minister says. Germany, Austria, Russia, all the great nations, consider actual service in the field should begin when a man reaches the age of twenty years, and 1 do not see why we should not follow their examule.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
In the United States,
the age is twenty-one.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
In the United States, the young men do not mature so fast as they do in Canada, and they are not as hardy. There is much .in the suggestion of calling out the three classes together. I have been endeavouring, since I have read this Bill, to visualize what will happen when it goes into force. I thought I had the right animal by the ear when I concluded that every man who belongs to the class concerned and who reads the proclamation, when he finds that he has to go and serve, immediately reports himself to somebody.
I thought I was right when I said that that somebody was the local tribunal. I was informed, however, that it was not. The man must report to some person who will take his name, address and so on, and who will make out his papers. Possibly there is a section providing that where nothing else applies, the Militia Act applies, and the Militia Act will apply with reference to enrolment. I think that is really what occurs, although the Solicitor General did not seem to be clear upon that point. As soon as the proclamation is issued, the man reports to some militia officer in his municipality or to the mayor, if there is no militia officer. The proclamation could appoint the mayor.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Look at section 13.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
Subsection 1 of section
13, says that the Militia Act will apply where nothing else does. LTnder the Militia Act, the Government could appoint men in all parts of the country, and the conscripts could report first to these offi-

cers, and then, if they desired to apply for exemptions, they would have to go before a tribunal which would be similar to a court of revision. I was not clear on that point before, but I am very glad to understand it now, and I think the House will understand the matter from what the Solicitor General has said. The man must first of all report to some person, officer, or non-commissioned officer, appointed under the Militia Act, give his name, address, age and other particulars, and then get his papers. If he wants an exemption, then he must make application or have somebody make application on his behalf to the local tribunal.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
He does not report
through that officer.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: No, but he can certainly state his objection to the officer, and he will he told to go to the tribunal with any objection he has. Is that corrects

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: It is likely that the tribunal will sit before the day for reporting, so that the man can have his application in before he reports.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: I think it would be better to have all the men report first, and then you would have a complete record of them.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: The hon. member has been giving explanations about the Bill. Perhaps he might explain what class the divorced man would come into. Would he come into the class of unmarried men or widowers? What class would the man judiciously separated as to bed and hoard come into?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
I am not in charge of the Bill, but I would say that the divorced man would come under the category of unmarried men, because the Divorce Bills passed in this House state that a man, once he is divorced, is unmarried.
I wish to discuss the case of the married man who has a young family. I think the older married men, that is those from thirty-five to forty, should be taken before the married men from twenty to thirty. The younger married man generally has a very young family dependent upon him. His children are not of such an age that they can take care of themselves. Therefore, if you are going to take the married men, you should take first the married man who is likely- to have a grown-up family. A married man of from thirty-five to forty will usually have some children who are old enough to take care of their mother in case something happens.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
That depends upon
when the man gets married.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Men get married fairly young these days. Every commanding officer within the sound of my voice will agree with me that one thing that touches us all is that sometimes we have in the ranks fathers with three or four small children at home dependent upon them. The separation allowance does not provide sufficient for those children. The State could well afford a certain amount monthly for each child instead of stating a lump sum. There should be a lump sum for the mother and then five or ten dollars a month for each child. We are not, however, discussing that; we are discussing the categories. I trust the minister in charge of the Bill will give very serious consideration as to whether the Bill had not better provide that when you are going to take a married men's class you should take, first, men over thirty instead of men under thirty. In regard to the marrying section, I would like the minister to consider whether it is exactly according to Hoyle that no one who is going to 'be conscripted is to be allowed to get married. That is virtually what happens, because it is stated that unmarried men who get married after a certain date will not be considered as married within the meaning of this Act.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Will not that be against morality and public order?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: I do not think this Parliament should put any obstacle in the way of a man getting married. At Valcartier I was strongly against any young man who was going to the war getting married, and I would not allow many young men to get married. After I reached England I found that the people there held different views, and they were endeavouring to encourage every young man who was going to the war to get married. I came to the conclusion finally that that was the correct idea,

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: What is the practice in Prance?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
The same as in England. Every young man, before he goes to the war, is supposed to get married. The matter is one of the protection of the race as well as anything else, and it was discussed pro and con in the English papers. The people there finally decided to encourage and permit all their young men to get married before they went to the war. As I said before, I changed my views on the subject, and I subsequently permitted every young

man under my care who wished to- get married to do so. I hope this measure will not throw any obstacle in the way of any man getting married, and if he gets married I hope he will be put in the married men's class. There are not enough men getting married nowadays.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
In view of the objections that the Solicitor General has raised to merging the first three classes, and in view of the .possibility of igetting sufficient men in the first class, I think the suggestion offered by the hon. member for North Perth (Mr. Morphy) was a very good one, that is, that class 2 should be called first, and either class three or class 1 following class 2. In the event of enough men being called out under class 1, I can hardly imagine that battalions of mere youths would be as desirable as would battalions in which older men were intermingled with younger men. As the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Taylor) has pointed out, the older men would add some ballast to the younger men.
And I am sure, from) what I have seen my-' self, that older, men placed alongside the younger men would be a very great advantage indeed. 1 do not think it would be advisable to call out those under 23 ,or 24 years of age first, if there was any possibility of getting the required number of men from that class. I can hardly help feeling that the first call of say 50,000 men would be met in that class. I think there are surely a sufficient number of men in that class who -are eligible, and who have no claims to exemption, to bring the number up to at least 50,000, and personally I would not like to see battalions of mere youths drafted, and older men left at home.
I think the suggestion of the hon. member for North Perth (Mr. IMorphy) that class 2 should be called first is a very good one, in view of the objections the hon. the Solicitor General has put forth to merging the three classes.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: I would like to Tepeat my question to the Solicitor General although of course the member for North Simooe (Mr. Currie) gave me an answer. Take the case of a man in the province of Quebec who is separated as to bed and board, where the wife is given entire charge .of the children. Would such a man, if he remains married, be placed in the category of married men, and exempt in cases where married men would be exempt, or would he placed in the category of widowers?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: I should say that is not a -matter of administration, but rather a matter fpr the interpretation of the judiciary. To my mind the man referred to by the hon. gentleman is still married. A judicial separation does not dissolve a marriage.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
Should not the Act -be amended to include him?
Mr. iMBIGIHEN:	I do not think so, because his domestic obligations, may exist just the same. I do not think we should keep refining the Act for the sake of two, or three, or even half a dozen men. I wish to draw this to the attention of hon. members-let us not be worrying ourselves too much by the fear that there will be a .tremendous and immediate result from any cause. If suc-h should be the case, it would be very different frqm what took place in Great 'Britain, and I do not know of any reason why we can expect such a very pronounced and enthusiastic response and absence of application for exemption in Canada, in contrast with what took place in Great Britain. It would appear to me to be rather likely on examination of the conditions there, as to nearness to the war, and conditions here as to that and many other things, that the contrast would likely be the other way. Most earnestly I hope it will not be so. Still, let us not worry ourselves in this House by the dream of possibilities that are not warranted by the experience of countries which have tried the selective draft system. In Great Britain, the experience was that the number of applications for exemptions far exceeded all expectations, and the number of exemptions exceeded the expectations by a large percentage. Only by a. tightening up of the Act, by regulation and by amendment, and by a strict and severe system of appeal, were they able to obtain the men they expected to obtain (from the beginning. Here' in Canada, have we reason to believe from the record of our voluntary enlistment, as compared with Great Britain, that we are going to get results far more favourable and far more satisfactory than they achieved there? Grand though our record is, I am afraid we cannot boast it is better than the experience of Great Britain.
That being the position, we have every reason in the world to anticipate that we will require all the available men in the first three classes. "Available" is a term which has no very exact meaning. It is a term that may mean one thing or another. We want the 100,000 best available men.

We think we can get the 100,000 best available men under the provisions of this Bill, consequently the working out of the Bill and the getting of them, believing that we will have the whole first three classes to comb through at all events, is to divide them into classes in order that the machinery which we here provide may not be unnecessarily congested. We may call them out just as quickly as we like, and we may call out class 2 ahead of class 1, if we wish.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Then, why not do it?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
Because the Act is all right as it is. There is no sound reason for it, and what reason there is would be against it. At least, that is my judgment. But, supposing I am wrong, it will come to the same thing in the end. The classes will be called in such order as will be most expeditious and consistent with the efficient working of the machinery, and we hope to get the best available men out of each of these first three classes. I would ask the committee not to refine unnecessarily in this matter. We will'undoubtedly need all the men we can get.
What new spirit has come over the House which makes it feel that we can come to the conclusion there are far more men in this country than we will need for the war? We will need them all. We will need this 100,000 men, and we will need them as quickly as we we can get them. I hope we will never need any more. When w-e come to get 100,000 more, after the voluntary enlistment we have had, we will not find them coming to us pell-mell. Our experience will be the experience of the older countries, and we must unite, and try to get the men, or at least have the machinery to get them in the most efficient way.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: I do not want to be considered too obtrusive in this, but I rather made up my mind to-night that the invitation of the Government to this committee to' make suggestions was merely a play upon words.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
If the hon. gentleman
will permit me to get from this clause to some others, I will convince Mm by actual acceptance of suggestions that it was nothing of the kind. I am sure I do not wish to impose my will on the committee, but I do not want the Act to be altered for no purpose in such a w.ay that it will result in the unfortunate working of the machinery of the Bill. We get the purpose that hon.
gentlemen have in mind under the Act as it is. There is no other object that can be served. Consequently, it becomes a .matter of the smooth working of the Act, nothing more and nothing less. Suggestions have been made which have been found very valuable, and I propose to recommend their acceptance to the House.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: I was'dealing with this one just now, and this will be my last word on it. Taking every word the Solicitor General has said, and it is an argument in favour of the proposition made by other members of this committee, if he is right that it will take the three classes then no difference will be made in this selection by combining them. If he be right in saying that it will take the three, there is no reason why he should not take them at once except the little inconvenience if any, that will be caused. If he is wrong, then he is going to call out boys from 20 to 24 before be calls out the others.	'	.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
We could not take
them altogether in any event by calling out the three at once:	It will be the appeal tribunals, who, by the severity or leniency of their interpretation of the exemption clauses, will decide just how many we get. Secondly, we hope we shall get on with a not too severe application of the Act. We will apply it equally everywhere. That will be the controlling idea. We are going to utilize the whole three classes.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: If you are going to take the whole three classes why do you not do it at once? The Solicitor General argues from my point of view every time he speaks. If it is so that he will take the three classes he has not presented any argument at all for not taking the three classes at once except that of a little inconvenience. He might do away with that by calling them out at 9, 10 or 11 o'clock . or Mondays, Tuesdays or Wednesdays.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: They have to report at different times.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: That may be so but at the most it is only a little inconvenience and I do not think the committee takes that argument seriously. It is not a serious matter compared with the result of denuding the country of its boys of from 20 to 24 while these other men are not required to go over.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: There is no possibility of that. .

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: That is the hon. gentleman's -opinion, and he is entirely free to express it, but he is wrong.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: It is not a matter of opinion at all. Whether I am right or wrong, the Government can call out the whole three classes and take the most available men of the three. That is the intention.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
The Solicitor General
says for the first time that that is the intention. He contended all along that that could not be done. He never said that it was' the intention to use the whole three classes for the first 50,000.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: I venture to say that I have said it half a dozen times.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: I have been trying during the three or four times that I was on my feet to get the hon. gentleman to say that. If he does that he can put them into one class. There is no reason for not putting them into one class.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Except the matter of convenience which is very important.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
The matter of convenience enters into it very little, if at all. We are leaving it in the hands of the tribunal or the Government to say whether they will call out class one first and get the whole
50,000	out of that class. The refusal of this suggested change by the Solicitor General does not give us the guarantee that we would like to have that they would treat these three classes as one. I will not vote for that clause in the Bill as it stands now because there is no reason, except the paltry excuse which has been given by the Solicitor General, for leaving it there.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
I would like to ask the Solicitor General to take a totally different view. I cannot understand his view when he says that it is for convenience that the classes have been placed in this way. Convenience would be furthered by combining the three classes from 20 to 34 years of age. Doing away with two classes would simplify the Bill.
Mr. MEIGHEN >
The Bill would be simpler but the working out of the Bill would be much more difficult. If they were all in one class they would have to be called together; consequently they would have to Teport together supposing they did not get exemptions. That would congest the reporting and cause unnecessary delay on the part of those waiting for their turn for per-

haps days. Consequently, it would congest the local tribunals before whom applications for exemptions were being made and heard. Hon. gentlemen may entertain the opinion that there will be no inconvenience. On this matter the officers of the Militia Department have been consulted. They regard very seriously this matter of convenience. The question of compensation to applicants for certificates of exemptions pending the determination of their cases has been under consideration. It has been decided that it be not granted; otherwise it would be in the Bill. The introduction of anything which will create inconvenience is opposed very strongly by those who have to do with the working out of the Act. There will be delays, men will be kept 10 or 20 miles away from their avocations and if we have the three classes apply at once there will be unnecessary inconvenience to the individual and unnecessary expense to the country. That is the argument as to convenience. There can be no question about that, at all events, to my mind. Of course, I would agree with my hon. friend from Perth (Mr. Morphy) that that would be met just as well by putting crass two where class one is. There would be ho difference one way or the other, but the congestion which would be caused by calling the three classes together is to be avoided.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
It is difficult to speak
very specifically on matters dealing with the man-power of the country, but as plainly as I can speak, I want to do- so. The reason that moved me to suggest that the classes toe reversed and that the- older unmarried men and widowers without children be taken before the boy of 20 is that I can point to town after town where the pool rooms and picture shows are filled with young men from 24 and 25 years of age, while the boys of 18 and 20 have gone to the front. I want to reach that class. If the Solicitor General will utilize his undoubted ability in some way to- reach that class he will give great satisfaction to the country. I do not think -it is fair to put through a Bill which on the face of it calls from a good home the young fellow who has reached 20 years of age and forces him into the limelight as a conscript, when men of the class that I have mentioned all over the -country, men who drive -their motors, frequent pool rooms-, go to the picthre shows-, enjoy all kinds- of amusements and have no patriotic spirit, are left at home. These are the men that I want to get after and they are the ones that I want to get

after first. If there is to 'be any class singled out, it should 'be the men who should have gone to the front at first and not the young fellow with green bones who is growing up and who, will be taken out of . a good home while, these fellows are going around in idleness and making fun of the war.

speechtext:
There is a part of the community that we should not forget, and that part is represented by the pedlars. I refer to the pedlars 'who have gone from Canada to the United States, the pedlaTS Who have come from England to Canada, and the pedlars who are- in the army. We see them in Montreal and elsewhere. They pass from one regiment to the other. My hon. friend from Perth (Mr. Morphy) says that he wants to get after the young fellows who go to the picture shows, I would like to get after the deserters from the army. We have had a wastage of 73,000 in the army, half of which is due to unavoidable causes and the other half -to deserters.
The hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) referred to an editorial in a Detroit newspaper welcoming 17,000 Canadian boys. Where did these boys -come from? They came from Canada. We have heard a lot about slackers. I shall never give the name oE slacker to a man who has not enlisted, but who has remained in Canada. But the man who has gone from Canada to the United States 'in order to evade military service I would call a slacker, and if we are honest and sincere in our desire to get after slackers why not get after the 17,000 in Detroit, and, perhaps, another 17,000 in other cities not far from the boundary. What are they doing there? They are not working; they have some one to pay their board; they are well-off people from Canada, rich men's sons. We have some slackers here from England to be found in insurance offices in Montreal. Going into these offices one would think he was in the city of London, from hearing their language. They do not ask for a salary; they are supposed to be working on commission, but they do not care if they put on one, or two, or three insurances per month, -as they receive their cheques from home. These are slackers. But -we have something more. I have here the immigration report of the United 'States. In 1913 the emigration from Canada to the United States was 43,000, in 1914 it was
43.000,	in 1915 it was 59,000, an increase of
16.000,	and in 1916 it was 85,000. It is no wonder that the Detroit paper speaks of
17,000	Canadians when you have in two
209i
years an increase of 58,000 over the normal emigration from Canada to the United States. Are we going to let these boys stay there, these pedlars men who go from one regiment to another, or from one country to another? These young men will not serve in the United States or in Canada. They are beautiful boys, 'strong and healthy. Why not take some stepis to get them back? The man in -Canada to-day should not he called a slacker, but every man who went to the United States to avoid military service deserves that name, and the difference in the immigration figures before and since the outbreak of war shows conclusively that these men went there for the purpose of avoiding military service. The day after the Prime Minister announced conscription there were 73 applications in one office in Montreal for passports to enable boys to go to Mexico. They were not going thqre to work. These young men have stayed in our country, but this incident shows that we have a part of our population who will go anywhere to avoid military service. These Canadians who have gone to the United States1 retain all the rights of British citizenship, and when -conscription is being introduced into .Canada -the first duty of the Government should be to bring these men back. The Government should also go after the deserters who make up a part of the shortage of 73,000 men. I kiy>w that some of these men are in some of o-ur parishes, and notice should 'be given that they are liable to punishment.

speechtext:
The Solicitor General in arguing -against the combination of these three classes quoted the British Royal Aviation Service as taking men under twenty-five. That is quite right, but the reason given by them was that the young man under twenty-five was likely to take greater-chances. Besides that, he had to have an intricate knowledge of a certain kind of machinery, and everybody knows that the younger a man is, practically speaking, the -more apt he is to pick up knowledge of machinery, because he is not so set in his views, or he has not had a training in some other line of business. He is apt to learn more quickly the organism of the m-a-chine he has to manipulate, and is much more apt to take hazardous chances, I understood from the men who were recruiting that_ that was why they wanted younger men. In addition to that, younger -men were lighter. Anybody familiar with -athletics knows that the younger a man is the better athlete he generally makes, provided he- is over 18 years of age, because his bones are not so hardened, and he can be trained into greater activity. I refer tp the foot runner -and the field -athlete. They are more amenable to training and can be more serviceable for that reason. Any one who has had experience in training in any walk of life knows that the man who has his growth, and whose bones are set for every day plodding work, is- more matured than the young man from 20 to 23 years- of age. 'My hon. friend from West Sim-coe told us what -the regular army in Germany was. I have seen a great -many people from Germany in my time, and I have read a great deal about the German army, but I do not believe anybody else has ever said that the first -German army was -composed, of men from 20 to 22. I am quite sure I never heard it before, although my hon. friend read it out of a book. That was their ages when they were enlisted, hut are not retired till they are 45, and I have no doubt the German guards, the greatest of the German soldiers, is -composed of -men of more mature years. The hon. gentleman from North Simcoe also stated that these young 'Canadians were br-ave and made good soldiers. There has- been no suggestion or hint that they are not. We all agree that they have done nobly, but there is no possible doubt that they are not as safe, when exposed to the temptations of -military life, as the imen of more mature years, -and there is no doubt there was more sickness, according to Dr. Bruce's report, among the younger men than among the older men.
I absolutely agree with my hon. friend from 
New Westminster (Mr. Taylor) who has had the experience, apparently, that if these three classes were combined they would make a steadier army. The -Solicitor General asks, what reason have we to suppose that there would -be 50,000 men to be got from the first class? I ask, what reason have we to suppose that there would not be 50,000 men obtained from the first class? Suppose there were a great many applications for exemption, what reason have we to suppose the tribunal would allow those exemptions, because those are the very class ihat are not in a fixed avocation? I do not believe that the tribunals would allow those men to be exempted to such an extent as they would perhaps exempt the older men. No reason has been given by the -Solicitor General, from start to finish, why the three classes should not be combined, except for convenience of registration and convenience of exemption. I have not the slightest idea that the registration will have to be done in one day, no matter how many classes are-called out. I have no hesitation in thinking that whoever makes the regulations will have sense enough not to make them all register in one day, but will give a number of days for the registration, -and a number of days for applications for exemption. There is no need whatever to have all the men apply on the one day for exemption or registration.

I beg pardon, it would not have the same result. They would all be called at the same time, but the notices would state that men between certain ages would register between certain dates. If the Solicitor General will tell us definitely that some system of that kind will be provided in the regulations such as he suggested a few days ago, it will be quite satisfactory, but why not have it in the Bill and let the regulations provide, as they do a great many other things in the Bill, how

they shall he called out, and make them all one class. The Solicitor General may know more about law than the ordinary man, but other people have just as good ideas as to the number of men that will be called out, under these classes, as he can possibly Rave, and he will be more than surprised at the number of men who will be liable to be called in that first class in every town and city in this country, and if they are all exempted, of course he will not get the desired number. However, I take it for granted the tribunals will use common sense in theiT exemptions.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: It can be done as my hon. friend suggests, by grouping the three classes, and leaving the regulations to divide them.
