speechtext:
That, in effect, is the same as it is now. It is the intention of the Government, as I have already stated several times, that the whole three classes shall be resorted to, because we believe that will be necessary in order to get the
100,000	men, without interfering unnecessarily with industry. I am very glad to hear the remarks of the hon. gentleman from Oxford; because I know he is sincere, and he believes _that the 100,000 men can be procured quite easily without interfering with industry at all, and without taking any of those who, in the national interest, are better , at home, but he must remember that for days, for weeks and for months in this House, hon. members who sit not very far from him have told us over and over again, in language of more or less menace, and very much verbal force, at all events, that we could not get more men in this country without denuding our population of its productive element, without interfering with agriculture, and without interfering with industry of every kind to a serious extent, from the point of view of prosecution of the war.
The member for North Oxford is more nearly right than were those hon. gentlemen. 'I was glad ,tb hear that expression of opinion from him. I myself think that we can get the 100,000 men without any diminution of production, but I do not see that we will get them so very easily without more applications for exemption than the hon. gentleman anticipates.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
It is surprising that
the Solicitor General should inform the committee to-night that it is intended to call out the three first classes.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: I have said that from the beginning.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
Not at all. But we have a still higher authority than the Solicitor General. We have the authority of the Prime Minister, who made an entirely different statement to this House on July 7.
I took the liberty then of saying that it was most injudicious that the young men from 20 to 23 should be first called out for service, and it was argued by the Prime Minister and the Solicitor General that that was the class of men that could best be spared. The inference to be drawn from their argument was that it was in the best interests of the country that these young men should be first called out. It was contended that they would make the-best soldiers, that they could best be' spared from the industries, that they were-not settled down in various occupations. What did that mean,? It meant that if the-number of men required could be obtained: from the men of the first class, the second class would not be touched, nor would the third, the fourth, or any of the remaining classes. Let me read what the Prime Minister said on that occasion. Referring to some remarks which I had made, he said:
If my hon. friend has any better suggestion which will commend itself to our judgment we are prepared to consider it. Would it be worth while to place all those between 20 and 35 in one class, call them out at once, and, perhaps, get 300,000, or 400,000, or 500,000, when we really only want 100,000? We may get 100,000 men in the first class.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: He did not say he expected to.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
He did not say he expected to? When the Prime Minister, who is responsible for this Bill, who has presented to the House figures with reference to our population, says: we have established ten classes; we purpose taking them in the order in which they are placed on the statute, but we may get the whole! 100,000 from the first class; are we to assume that he meant what he said? Yet the Solicitor General says: Oh, he did not say he would be likely to get the required number from the first class. The statement of the Prime Minister meant that all the men required would be taken from the first class if they could be got. Yet, the Solicitor General, after the strong arguments presented tonight by members on both sides, says: Oh, we will get over that, because we may at 9 o'clock in the morning call out the first class, at 10 o'clock call out the second class.

and at 11 o'clock call out the third class; it is only for convenience that we have arranged these different classes. His statement is a surprising one, and entirely at variance writh the statement made by the Prime Minister a few evenings ago. The Solicitor General says that to adopt the suggestion of the member for North Oxford would be doing the very thing that this Bill allows to be done. But what the member for North Oxford says is this: the call would be upon all these three classes if they were united in one, and for convenience those of a certain age might register in one booth and those of another age in another. That does not mean that the men would be in three separate classes; it means that they would all be called out together, but that, for convenience of registration, or reporting, they would be allowed to report at different places, according to their age. The same result might be accomplished in another way, perhaps more conveniently. Those whose names begin with certain letters, say from A to G, could register at one place, those from G to M in another, and so on-speaking, if you like, of the same village or parish. Notwithstanding what the Solicitor General has said, this Bill imposes a first obligation upon the young men between the ages of 20 and 23 years inclusive. The second obligation is upon those from 24 to 28 inclusive, and so on up to 40 years of age. It seems to me that the three classes should be united in one, just as was wisely done under the Militia Act, and that the unmarried men should also be united in one class. This should be insisted upon until the Bill is amended in order to meet the view of the majority of the committee. If this Bill passes, the Solicitor General will have no power by regulation or otherwise to avoid imposing the first duty upon the first class. Upon the first class will rest the call to active service. If an insufficient number of men are obtained by that call, then the second class would !be called upon. As the Prime Minister said, it might not he necessary to call upon the
11 p.m. men of the second class; that class could be divided into two sub-classes, one of which could be called first. No power on earth-central appeal judge, Solicitor General, Governor in Council-can alter the meaning and intention of the Bill if it is allowed to pass in its present form; that is, that the first obligation shall rest upon the young men between the ages of 20 and 23 inclusive.

There is one thing
about this Bill that so- far I have not been quite able to understand. This measure is called by the Government and by the people throughout the country " Selective Conscription." I have not been able to find the selective element in the Bill or in the machinery that is about to be put into force. The term " Selective Conscription " as understood in the United States means that the men are selected for their physical attainments and other reasons, and the Government secures, out of the men who have registered, a selective class to fill up the number they require. As I 'understand this Bill, on a certain day, a call goes out for all the men of class 1 to register at certain places. They come and they register. Every man who registers is supposed to be [DOT]drafted into a battalion and go through the necessary steps until he reaches the front. Up- to that stage, there is no selection at all.

speechtext:
That is in the United
'States?	. '	[DOT]

No, here. The man who registers, has enlisted, practically the same as if he has volunteered. That is the end *of the matter. Unless he .appeals to this tribunal, he goes through the various steps until he reaches the front. I cannot find any selection so far. The only selection would be if the, man appeals. If nobody appeals, there is no selection. Where does the selective element come in? Perhaps the minister will tell me what he understands by selection. I do not regard appealing and the decision by the Court of Appeal, as selection at all. That is merely the result of a man protesting in a certain way against going, and appealing to the court and the court sustaining his protest. I fully agree with the views put forward by the hon. member for North Perth (Mr. Morphy) as to the class of men that we .should first select. I do not take all the
grounds that the hon. member put forward, such as that many of them are idlers. That may be. I argue on the ground that we get the better class of men from the ages mentioned by the hon. member for North Perth, and that we should leave the others for the present until they reach a maturer age. What I particularly want to point out to the minister is in regard to the idea that-the Government by their own act shall select the men who should go and leave out the men who should not go. So far as 1 have heard the discussion, there is no machinery per se in the Act itself.

I am assuming that after this measure becomes law, there will probably be a short opportunity for voluntary enlistment. On that assumption I wish to put a suppositious case to the Solicitor General for the purpose of inquiring whether the point has ever been before him for consideration. Suppose, immediately after the call was made, two men of military experience advised the Minister of Militia that they could each recruit a battalion of 1,250 men, making a tptal of 2,500 men, the proportion assignable tb Nova Scotia under that suppositious case, what would be the policy of the Government in such circumstances? made under the Act? Would the province have credit for the number s.o voluntarily enlisting, and would the call under the Military service Act be postponed or abated or discontinued altogether until the next call was issued. Mr. MEIiGHEN: And there is no intention of discriminating between provinces at all. The Act does not deal with the Dominion as so many provinces; it deals with the Dominion of Canada as a nation. Still the Government statistician who prepared the figures isays: " the figures of the table are those of the census of 1911, and it is estimated that the increase since 1911 in the male population of Canada of ages 20 to 45 lies 'between 300,000 and 400,000. As approximately this number has been already recruited, the figures of 1911, it is thought, reflect rather closely present conditions in the Dominion as a whole." It therefore seems to me it is not unreasonable that I should take these figures as a basis for my argument. When the young man of twenty applies for exemption he will be met by the question: " Why should you be exempt?" The only reason he can give as to why exemption should prevail in his case would toe this: " in the national interest I am entitled to be exempted." The tribunal will say: " on what particular grounds should you be exempted?" The young man of twenty has not chosen his avocation in life, his proclivities have not been determined, and he will find himself ' in this embarrassing position that because he has not had an opportunity of selecting some definite line of work in which he is perfecting himself, the tribunal will likely say: " the work you intend to undertake, or the work you have undertaken, is not of such a character that it should be considered as in the national interest. You need not continue in it, you must be considered a recruit."
If the figures I have read are 'an approximation, and I think they are if the statistician is correct, it is possible the whole
100,000	men may be taken from the first class, and the second class not called up at
all. In my judgment this would be radically unfair.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
According to the Militia
Act single unmarried men are called first up to the age of 45. I see by clause 4 that married men and widowers with children from 20 to 34 are called before single men and married men from 34 to 45. The calling out of married men imposes a heavier burden on the country, -because it has to take care of their wives and children. Would it not be possible to take unmarried men up to the age of 40 before touching the married men and widowers with children?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
That, as almost all
other suggestions, was debated in the committee when this clause was first up. The reason for the classification which has been made is that the best military age is broadly from 20 to 35. After 35 there ie a marked deterioration; consequently, it urns felt that all below that should be accepted first.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: I put a question to the Solicitor General in respect to this selective element that is in -the present Bill, I did not get an answer because my hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. Maclean), by reason of his superior right intervened. Now that the point mentioned by my hon. friend is over -and done with, possibly the Solicitor General would answer me.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: There may be a measure of correctness, speaking from the point of view of the philosopher, in the point of my -hon. friend. The selective clauses are the clauses which relate to exemptions. The operation of those clauses will be of itself the selection. It is quite true that with respect to those who enrol themselves and do not themselves make any application or suggestion to the local tribunals that in the national interest they be exempt, or in respect to whom no such application is made, there is no specific operation of any selective clause. But that -proceeds on the principle that if the man himself does not suggest by way of application to -the local tribunal that he should be -exempt, and if no one does it on his behalf, there is a fair and reasonable assumption that the selection would not exempt him. Consequently, practically speaking, the selective principle permeates the whole Bill.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: As I understand the hon. gentleman's answer, there is no selection at all. The Government accepts everybody who comes along, everybody who will write his name down as being within a certain class. The Government do not reject anybody but take everybody..

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
Clause 3 stands. Now, we are at clause 4. As to clause 4 a suggestion was made by the leader of the Opposition and also it was made independently by hon. members on this side of the House and pressed, I remember, by the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Taylor) that there should be a diversion of jurisdiction between the Militia Service Act and the Army Act on one hand and this Act on the other, that the line should be clearly fixed where the Militia Service Act ceases to operate, as it were, in regard to prosecutions and penalties and where the Army Act commences to operate. It was urged that there should not be -an alternative jurisdiction and it was further urged by the hon. member for Perth (Mr. Morphy) that there should be a more severe penalty. Careful consideration has been given to the proposals and I wish to suggest .to the committee that the suggestions be met in this way: That sub-clause 4 of section 4 of the Bill be amended to read as follows:
Any man who is called out, and who without reasonable excuse fails to report as aforesaid, shall be guilty of absenting himself without leave, and shall be liable, on summary conviction, to imprisonment for any term not exceeding five years with hard labor.
The result is that we create here only the offence of absenting -himself without leave as committed by the man who fails to report and who is made liable to report under this Bill.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Why use the term "absent without leave" because "absent without leave" under the Army Act is a different thing altogether. Why not say "refuses to report? Absence without leave is treated by the commanding officers constantly and a man^ is fined for a few days' absence. A confusion of terms might arise.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: I do not think the name is very important; in fact, it might be just as well to call it an offence. It seems to me to be fully the same offence as that committed by the man who, having enrolled, absents himself without leave. Consequently, I think the name is quite appropriate, but if we simply called it an offence the effect would -Be exactly the same.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: That leaves out paragraph (a) altogether?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
Yes, it leaves o-ut the
creation of the offence by this Bill that he who-, having reported, does not remain o-n active service where placed, leaving that offence to- be taken care of by the Army Acit. There is another alternative jurisdiction. He is between the civil and military t-ri-

b,imals/ and the line is clearly drawn between the operation of the Army Act and this 'Act. The punishment for absenting himself without leave is made five years with hard labour. It was thought that as no one could commit the offence except a man who wias physically fit for military service that punishment would suit him.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: You increase the penalty from three years to five years?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: On the well-known principle of making the punishment fit the crim-e. It is hoped that this will have a greater preventive effect.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
Does failing to go and
register constitute the offence with which the minister is dealing?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
Failing to report if it
is his duty to report under this Act.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: There is another matter involved. There should be the greatest certainty that the individual has had notice before he is subjected to punishment. This is similar to the offence of contempt of court in the case of a juror or witness, and in such a case the-judge requires very clear evidence that the individual has had notice. The mere proclamation of the Military Service Act would not be sufficient to justify us in treating ias a criminal a man who did not obey all its provisions.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: The effect would be that the Government would have to assume responsibility for that notice reaching every man in the country. I do not think if my hon. friend were a member of a Government he would -cane to assume that responsibility. If it should be shown to- a judge that the person charged was n-o't aware o-f the proclamation or had no notice of his duty, that fact might be pleaded by way of excuse, and it would be for the judge to decide.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
Where must he report,
to the military authorities?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Under the Militia Act.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
In the administration of
the l^w, I think that these -men should be compelled first to serve in the army and then to serve their term in prison. If a man wanted -to avoid going to the war he might prefer to take his chance of getting two or three years in the penitentiary, with good food and -clothing and perhaps a little stone breaking, which is not as hard as trench work, to going to the front. I had a letter from a 'Canadian who got into trouble of this kind in the Old Country and
who was finally given two years; but he had first to join the -conscript army and go to the trenches. If a -man is capable of service he should not be relieved of his obligation to serve simply because he stays away and a magistrate sentences him to a year in prison.
Then account should be taken of the large number of men who are enlisted in the militia and the Canadian defence force. They claim exemption under this Act. These men have enlisted under a valid contract for three years, and under the Militia Act are exempted from service abroad. I know a number of men under these -circumstances who say they are not liable under this Act. How is that condition to be -met under the Bill.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
Unless they are -also
members of the -Canadian Expeditionary Forces they are liable. Every one is liable except those who are exempted, and they are not exempted.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: How can the Government void that valid contract unless th-ese men are specifically mentioned. There -should be some clause distinctly stating that these men are not exempt. There was the same trouble in England. The territorials would not serve abroad, saying they had enlisted for three years for service at home and would not seTve abroad. The -Government had to disband the territorial regiments, and that threw these men back under the ordinary Act. It should be made clear that this Act applies to all men enlisted in the Canadian militia. 'The hon. member for St, John (Mr. Pugsley) said that this Bill will be interpreted not by this Parliament hut by the cpurts. A man will make a claim in the court, and unless the Act is clear on every point, the judges may rule against him. It is not the first time Parliament has passed a Bill and the judges have decided that it was not good law.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: As has been stated over and over again during the debate, our militia men, under the Militia Act, can serve beyond Canada. Therefore, our militia men can serve overseas.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Yes, but the proclamation under the Militia Act has not been made yet, and they are not liable to serve abroad until the proclamation has been made.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
The amendment I propose will make subsection 4 read as follows:
Any man who is called out, and who without reasonable excuse fails to report as aforesaid, shall be guilty of an offence, and shall be liable, on summary conviction, to imprison-

ment for any terra not exceeding five years j with hard labour.
That is the maximum penalty. It may he less.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
Would the Solicitor
General consider the advisability of inserting a provision that the mere fact of a man being sentenced under this section shall not release him from liability to serve under this Act? I think common sense would tell us that that would be a proper provision.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: A man once ma4e liable by an Act is not released until the Act says he is released. Consequently, a man does not release himself by violating the Act. In my opinion, the Act, as it stands, renders a man liable, after he commits the offence and serves the punishment, just as he was before. If, however, I should change my mind, I will bring the matter before the committee.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
Subsection 2 of section 4 reads:
Men so called out shall report, and shall be placed on active service in the Canadian Expeditionary Force.
In the case of a man who does not report, and is Sentenced to a term of imprisonment, he is not in the Canadian Expeditionary Force, not having reported, and they have no claim on him. In order to compel that man to go overseas, we must first make him a member of the Canadian Expeditionary Force. Under the present practice, a man who deserts, and is brought back, tried by a magistrate, and sentenced to a term of imprisonment, does not by that procedure, evade service with the force, but, when his battalion leaves for the front, he is taken from, prison, overseas, and compelled to, enter upon his military service there. It seems to me we should provide in this Bill that those who seek to evade service by getting into prison may be taken out of the prison, on the occasion of the first draft, and taken overseas.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Unless he is entitled to exemption.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
Those men do nut get exemption. Section 4 reads:
4. (1) The Governor in Council may from time to time by proclamation call "out on active service as aforesaid for the defence of Canada, either in Canada or beyond Canada, any class or subclass of men described in section three and all men within the class or subclass so called out shall, from the date of such proclamation, be deemed to be soldiers 
enlisted in the military forces of Canada and subject to military law for the duration of the present war, and of demobilization thereafter, save as hereinafter provided.
Whether he reports or not, the moment the proclamation issues that man is a soldier in the military forces of Canada, and subject to military law, and consequently, being a soldier, we can apply the hand of the law to him, just as much as we could to any other soldier, and if he does not report when it is his duty to report, it is the duty of the proper authorities to apply the physical hand of the law to him.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: There is this difficulty in the reasoning of -the hon. Solicitor General: that this man was a member of the military forces of Canada only, and the military forces of Canada are not, by this Bill, sent overseas. It is only the Canadian Expeditionary Force that goes overseas. This man, not having reported, is not a member of that force, according to subsection 2 of section 4.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: The subsection does not say that no one shall be placed on active service except those who report. It is the duty of the authorities to place these men on active service, and it is their duty to report. They will 'be placed on active service, whether they report or not, or whether they are brought to the proper place by the military authorities.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: These men not reporting may be tried in a summary manner, which means that any ordinary justice of the peace could send a man to the penitentiary for five years. I would seriously suggest of the minister that no less a personage than a county court judge, under the Speedy Trials Act, khould have authority. I do not think it is right that an ordinary magistrate, no matter how well meaning he may be, who knows very little about law, should be entrusted to the very serious duty of trying men, in circumstances of this kind. ,1 think they should be tried before a county judge.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
The summary convictions clauses of the Act provide for an appeal to a judge. It is true that, in cases involving intricate law, or substantial cases of law, the general scope or spirit of the legislation is to entrust that to the judges, but this will not involve consideration of law to .any very great extent. It would be a simple matter to decide whether the man was of the proper age, and if he was of the proper age, whether he had an exemption.

Then it is a mere matter of judgment as to tlie proper punishment. Of course, if a county judge tried all these eases it would, in one sense, be better. But we want to take care not to add too much formality or chance of delay or congestion to the enforcement of the Act.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: I would suggest that the hon. gentleman at least provide that these cases be tried before county court judges or stipendiary magistrates in cities and towns.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
I would suggest that we deal with this clause as we have dealt with some other clauses: that it be allowed to pass, and I will promise consideration myself, as well as to bring-it to the consideration of my colleagues. It can be spoken to later in the House.
Subsection 4 of section 4 agreed to.
Progress reported.

Wednesday, July 12, 1917.
